page: Microsoft Azure M32-16ms is a memory-intensive virtual machine belonging to the MS family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by a dedicated Intel Xeon 8280M processor operating at 2.7 GHz. The configuration provides 16 vCPUs across 8 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. It is equipped with 875.0 GB of system memory, translating to 54.69 GB of RAM per physical core. Local storage consists of a 1049 GB SSD, and the instance is Premium Storage capable.

Performance benchmarks indicate a clear division between single-core and multi-core capabilities. Single-core CPU performance is positioned in the bottom 25% according to stress-ng and Geekbench metrics, and single-threaded compression tasks like gzip and bzip3 register in the bottom 10%. However, multi-core CPU performance and multi-threaded decompression rise to average levels. Memory bandwidth tests, including read-only small block and large block operations, also yield average performance, though the Passmark memory score falls into the bottom 25%.

Given its massive memory footprint relative to compute resources, this server is designed for memory-bound workloads rather than compute-heavy tasks. It is highly suitable for large in-memory databases, caching layers, and enterprise applications requiring extensive RAM. Qualitative cost efficiency is characterized by high memory density, making it a specialized choice where RAM capacity is the primary constraint, despite the trade-off of lower single-core CPU performance.

The server is equipped with 875.0 GB of RAM, providing 54.69 GB of memory per core, alongside a 1049 GB local SSD with Premium Storage capabilities. Benchmark data shows weak single-core CPU and memory performance, but average multi-core and multi-threaded capabilities, including Redis SET operations and static web serving. This hardware profile is optimized for memory-bound workloads such as large in-memory databases, caching layers, and data-intensive enterprise applications where memory capacity is prioritized over raw single-core compute speed.
